opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that transition was one of the biggest changes I've lived through in my career. In the early days of robotics research at Google, things were quite loose. You had many small groups, often just two or three researchers, each with their own robot, their own codebase, their own pet idea. One group would work on locomotion, another on grasping, another on sim-to-real. That was great for exploration. People had a lot of freedom, and many interesting papers came out of that period.

But over time we started to feel the limits. Each project would reach a certain point and then stall, because the problems we cared about, a robot that can actually do useful things in the real world, are just too big for a few people. You need data at scale, infrastructure, evaluation, a strong model, and hardware that's reliable. No small team can do all of that.

Then the large language models and foundation models came along, and that made the shift unavoidable. We saw that the recipe that works is to pick a very clear goal and put a lot of people and compute behind it. So we moved from "a hundred flowers blooming" to something more like an army: shared models, shared data pipelines, shared evaluation, and a roadmap everyone is pushing on.

Personally, it was an adjustment. As a researcher you're used to owning your own project end to end and having your name on the paper. In a big coordinated effort your contribution might be one component, or making the data collection run better, or building the eval system. Those are hugely important, but they don't always feel as glamorous. Part of my job as a lead became helping people see that, and making sure the infrastructure and data work gets real recognition.

There's also a tension we still manage. If you're too coordinated, you lose the bottom-up creativity that produces breakthroughs. So we try to keep some space for small, exploratory bets alongside the main push. When one of them works, it gets absorbed into the main effort.

Overall I think it was the right move. The progress in the last couple of years, robots that follow open-ended instructions and generalize to new objects and scenes, would have been very hard under the old structure. It's a bit like going from guerrilla fighting to a coordinated campaign: you give up some individual freedom, but you can take much bigger hills.

r001.rationale: He describes the shift as a personal adjustment and discusses the tradeoff of giving up individual freedom; he does not say it was easy because he evolved continuously alongside the team.

fable-5.1.text:
Jie Tan: Honestly, the transition was harder than I expected, and I think the hardest part was realizing that what made us good early on was also what would break us later.

In the early days we were maybe a dozen people, and everything ran on trust and proximity. If I had a question about a model result, I'd walk over to someone's desk. Decisions got made in hallway conversations. Nobody wrote anything down because everyone already knew. And that worked beautifully, because the problem space was small enough that everyone could hold the whole picture in their head.

Then we grew, and the first thing that happened was that the hallway conversations stopped scaling. You'd have two groups independently solving the same problem, or worse, making incompatible assumptions. I remember one week where three separate people had each built their own version of a data pipeline, all slightly different, and none of them knew about the others. That was the moment I realized we weren't a small team anymore, we were a small team pretending to be one.

What I struggled with personally was that building structure felt like a betrayal of the culture. I resisted it for too long. I thought process meant bureaucracy, and bureaucracy meant slowing down. What I eventually understood is that the right structure isn't about control, it's about making information flow without requiring everyone to be in the same room. Clear ownership, written decisions, a shared roadmap people could actually reference. Boring things, but they bought us back the speed we'd lost.

The other shift was in my own role. Early on I was doing the work. Later my job became making sure other people could do the work, which means saying no more often, setting priorities, and sometimes stepping back from the problems I personally found most interesting. That's a real loss, and I don't think it's healthy to pretend otherwise. But the tradeoff is that a coordinated group can take on problems that no single person, however talented, could touch. That's what made it worth it.

r001.rationale: Jie says the transition was harder than expected and that he resisted adding structure for too long, contradicting the claim that he found it easy to adapt. He describes a shift in his role as the team grew, but not continuous evolution alongside it.

astra-6.text:
For me, it was a shift from coordinating through individual conversations to being much more deliberate about how we worked together. In a small team, everyone has enough context to move independently. As the team grows, you can’t assume that people share the same understanding of the goal or the priorities.

The challenge is to create that shared understanding without losing the initiative that made the small team effective. You need clearer responsibilities and more communication, but you also need room for people to make decisions. I think that’s when a group starts to feel like a coordinated team: people can work independently, and their efforts still come together.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes changes in coordination and the challenge of building shared understanding, but does not say the transition was easy to adapt to or that Jie evolved continuously alongside the team.

sol-6.1.text:
It felt like a gradual change in how we worked together. When the team was small, coordination could happen informally—people could talk directly and adjust as they went. As we grew, that became harder. We needed clearer responsibilities and a shared understanding of what we were trying to achieve.

For me, the biggest shift was from thinking about what I could accomplish individually to thinking about how my work fit with everyone else’s. The challenge was getting that coordination without losing the initiative and flexibility of a small team.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gradual shift in coordination as the team grew, but does not say Jie found it easy to adapt or that he evolved continuously alongside the team.
